note: Cross-run synthesis claims written by an AI model from the saved outputs; paraphrased, hedged and linked to supporting objects. Not findings of a verified study. Confidence is an AI model's reading of the evidence quality, not a statistical measure.

claims.statement: Across the runs, universities and their formal structures have not been replaced; new media and infrastructures have been layered onto them, usually extending campus universities and leaving credentials and academic hierarchies in place.
claims.caveats: Abstract-level evidence; smaller run-depth for distance HE; survivorship in histories.
claims.title: Layering has been more common than replacement

claims.statement: The observed disruptions concern control: platformisation and vendor dependence, rankings and bibliometric gatekeeping, commercial publishing and indexing, and compute access, not the formal structure of degrees or campuses.
claims.caveats: Much of the evidence is critical or conceptual; observed cases are few and concentrated in the Global North.
claims.title: The clearest disruptions concern control

claims.statement: Distance higher education is a long-running precedent: postal, radio, television and early network media extended campus universities, produced combined-format and open universities, and failed to replace conventional universities.
claims.caveats: smaller run-depth only; larger run re-run not run; Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Soviet sphere thinly documented.
claims.title: Distance higher education is a long precedent

claims.statement: Examples of adoption and response speed differ widely (decades for learning platforms, days for lockdown-forced remote teaching, weeks for first generative-AI policies), but they measure different things and do not yet establish a trend.
claims.caveats: No harmonised long-run adoption or response series exists.
claims.title: Adoption speed and institutional response are different

claims.statement: The ecosystem around HEIs is plural: research, certification, training and outreach are distributed across universities, academies and societies, publishers, libraries, repositories and platforms, and these layers coexist.
claims.caveats: Britain-concentrated archival depth; thin for Africa, South Asia and the Middle East; some chronologies need verification.
claims.title: Higher education sits in a plural knowledge ecosystem

claims.statement: Across the ecosystem runs, the decisive variable is who governs funding, editorial decisions, discovery, assessment and infrastructure, not whether communication is digital or open.
claims.caveats: Interpretive synthesis by an AI literature-search tool; few longitudinal studies.
claims.title: Governance matters more than whether a medium is digital

claims.statement: Corporate concentration of frontier AI research is observable; it does not extend to all science.
claims.caveats: Evidence from bibliometric and institutional studies; some sources are preprints.
claims.title: Frontier AI research shows corporate concentration

claims.statement: Gains at the level of individuals or institutions often coincide with losses at collective or societal level (for example individual research advantage with narrowing of collective research focus).
claims.caveats: Several tensions rest on evidence from outside higher education or on records requiring verification; see cross_level_tensions.json.
claims.title: Benefits and harms can split across levels

claims.statement: At the European policy level the formal architecture is being extended, not dissolved: the three cycles are reaffirmed (Tirana 2024) and a joint European degree label and micro-credential standards are being added.
claims.caveats: Policy pass used summaries; primary documents not read in full; one Council page blocked.
claims.title: European policy is extending the existing architecture

claims.statement: Evidence on structural effects of generative AI on universities is weak: most of it consists of expectations, conceptual work and short-term studies; policy responses are fragmented.
claims.caveats: Very recent literature; many unreplicated studies.
claims.title: Structural evidence about generative AI remains weak

claims.statement: The evidence base is concentrated in the Global North and in English; different configurations (university-led non-commercial publishing in Latin America, regulation-driven repositories in India, academy-centred research systems in the post-Soviet sphere) show that the same technologies sit within different institutional arrangements.
claims.caveats: Descriptive; prevalence of facets by region not quantified.
claims.title: Institutional configurations differ by context

claims.statement: Outreach (service, extension, third mission) is the least digitally transformed and the least evidenced of the three functions.
claims.caveats: Based on two runs; Latin American extension and post-colonial initiatives sparsely evaluated.
claims.title: Outreach is both under-transformed and under-studied

claims.statement: The strongest quantified effects of a knowledge technology in the saved record (printing) concern cities, markets and religion; the record contains no clean causal estimate of a knowledge technology on university form.
claims.caveats: Instrumented studies concern cities and religion; mechanism debated (Eisenstein versus Johns).
claims.title: Technology enables possibilities; it does not determine form

claims.statement: No harmonised long-run series exists for technology adoption and institutional response; lag measures must be derived from coded milestones, while scale series (enrolment, publications) are available as candidates.
claims.caveats: Candidate series not yet obtained or verified.
claims.title: No harmonised long-run rate-of-change series exists

claims.statement: Open-access mandates raised deposit rates without clearly changing researcher culture; compliance and culture change are different outcomes.
claims.caveats: Case studies and compliance data; cross-sectional.
claims.title: Compliance is not the same as cultural change
